## Abstract

This dissertation explores how the institutional design of state and local governance has

mediated the relationship between corporate power and local democracy in the United States. Across

three historical essays, I document how populist reformers during our first Gilded Age used state

constitutions and local government law to limit the democratic influence of local town bosses and the

industrial titans who had captured state-level governing institutions. In a final co-authored chapter, I

identify the consequences of specific changes in local government law that have facilitated the

proliferation of corporate enclaves across American metropolitan areas. These four essays draw from

the literatures and methodological approaches of legal analysis, historical institutionalism, comparative

political economy, democratic theory, and empirical social science. They use the historical

development of American industrial capitalism in the Gilded Age and Progressive Era as a primary

case to explore tensions between alternative conceptualizations of democratic self-governance: as (1)

community-level decisionmaking (local self-determination), or (2) freedom from the exercise of

arbitrary private power (anti-domination). I demonstrate that decentralization creates opportunities

for private domination by powerful firms both indirectly (through the structural power of mobile

capital and capture of public institutions) and also directly: through the facilitation of corporate

fiefdoms. As an intervention in theories of self-determination, I conclude that the democratic valence

of “local” control is contingent on the spatial concentration of taxable wealth and the institutional

design of metropolitan governance.

## Introduction

Last May, 218 residents of Starbase, Texas—almost all employees of Elon Musk’s aerospace

transportation company SpaceX or their family members—voted overwhelmingly to incorporate the

company’s landholdings into an independent and self-governed jurisdiction.1 The incorporation

represented the culmination of a yearslong effort by Musk first confirmed in a 2021 tweet on the social

media platform that he now owns: “Creating the city of Starbase, Texas.”2

Almost immediately after the incorporation vote, the company (operating through its new

shell government) took steps to consolidate its governing authority over a wide range of local

policymaking that affected its interests. The Starbase city commissioners—all of them current or

former SpaceX employees3—approved a request from SpaceX to cut off public access to the

community by installing gates, accessible only by access code, at points of entry.4 Although the new

city has legal authority to issue public debt, its initial operations were funded by a direct $1.5 million

loan from SpaceX, forgoing the legal processes and transparency mechanisms that typically

accompany the issuance of municipal bonds.5 Starbase has authorized the creation of a municipal

police force (headquartered in a building leased from SpaceX), and announced its intention to contract

with SpaceX itself for fire response and other municipal emergency services.6 The municipality has

signaled its intention to expand its jurisdictional boundaries by nearly tenfold: at a meeting in February,

Chapter 1: Regulating Location Incentives

My first chapter explores how this agrarian movement—long understood to have shaped

federal antimonopoly protections—was motivated in large part by widespread opposition to the

railroads’ domination of local economies (and politics) through structural power. Published as

“Regulating Location Incentives” in the Duke Law Journal (2024), this chapter demonstrates how

market structure—fair competition between firms—is distorted by inefficient location incentive

megadeals. It situates Tesla’s Texas takeover—and other examples, like Amazon’s HQ2 search and

Wisconsin’s Foxconn boondoggle—within the interdisciplinary literatures on urban governance and

fiscal federalism have extensively studied the “structural” power of mobile capital: firms’ ability to

influence local policymaking through anticipated exit threat. Towards that end, I draw parallels

between the current location incentive status quo and two historical episodes that shaped the

development of federal antitrust law.

I first demonstrate that the populist movement responsible for the enactment of our initial

antimonopoly protections was substantially motivated by opposition to the lavish incentives

demanded by private railroad companies, from competing towns, during the late 19th century. The

railroad trusts of that era—much like today’s dominant firms—were highly adept at converting their

economic leverage over vulnerable communities into political influence, that could then be converted

Researchers have documented the oppressive employment relationship in historical company

private fiefdoms had been maintained by requiring workers to reside within communities that were

owned (and therefore, controlled) by their employers. Proprietors of historical company-owned towns

demise of the company town. But parallel developments in local government law provided an

attractive alternative. I show that jurisdictional fragmentation has allowed its continuation through

new institutional forms, enabling corporate titans to wield public powers without accountability to any

broad public. Rather than exercising domination over captive worker-residents through private law,

employers increasingly adopted the public form—and then schemed to exclude from the voting

“demos” any residents who might oppose their prerogatives. This strategy (like the previous) centrally

historical company towns maneuvered to hold workers captive with the goal of compelling their

## Conclusion

The early U.S. Socialist Party’s municipal program, developed in the early twentieth century,

advocated expansive legal authority for municipalities as response to the corporate capture of state

and federal policymaking bodies. In a 1912 pamphlet “enumerati[ng] the various measures and lines

of constructive legislation that have been found of value by the Socialists in their work in municipal

government,” for example, the very first agenda item reads: “Complete home rule is demanded for

the city in all municipal affairs.”

During this period, transportation infrastructure and municipal utilities (like fire response and

water access) were often solely provided by extractive private companies; socialists and other

progressive reformers sought to expand local authority to directly provide these critical services

without interference from captured state politicians. Socialists campaigning for local office challenged

this form of corporate dominance through municipal ownership of public utilities and direct delivery


<!-- Page 28 -->


20

of public services.40  The vision was expansive: rural socialists in Oklahoma organized to challenge the

territory’s book trust—a corrupt publishing monopoly that bribed state officials to protect its scheme

charging families extractive fees for circularly-required textbooks—by using the 1907 constitution to

authorize city-owned print presses. But early socialists’ efforts to pursue these reforms were

consistently stymied by judicial declarations that their municipalities lacked authority to do so or

preemptive bills from state legislators—prompting the organizing demand for municipal home rule

and other legal expressions of city power. Indeed, New York City’s current (comparatively expansive)

home rule authority was originally secured by a 1924 constitutional amendment that was championed

by reformists like George R. Lunn, the four-term socialist mayor of Schenectady.

Those past efforts neatly preview current organizing agendas. Several democratic socialist

mayoral candidates have successfully mobilized electoral victories through similar campaign proposals,

including New York City’s Zohran Mamdani (promising to deliver on an affordability agenda through

city-run grocery stores) and Seattle’s Katie Wilson (proposing to expand the direct provision of

“Vienna model” social housing through a city-owned development fund). And just like earlier

socialists, contemporary New York City progressives still find their ability to deliver on core policy

proposals—and their governing success, more broadly—beholden to the whims of Albany.

Particularly under present conditions of geographic polarization, with Democratic voters concentrated

in urban metros while Republicans dominate among rural electorates, municipal empowerment—and

other variations of local control from state and federal preemption—is often imagined to be a core

progressive value.

But in this era of the corporate-dominated municipal enclave, “city power” can often

undermine popular self-governance—by providing the legal mechanisms for corporations (and their

The essays in this dissertation document the consequence of two connected developments in

local government law: increasing the availability of municipal incorporation (and minimizing the

corresponding democratic demands); and reducing the ability of major cities to annex wealthy enclaves

along their periphery. During the Gilded Age and Progressive Era, town bosses actively avoided the

municipal form: preferring to govern instead through the private law of property and contract,

displacing rather than capturing democratic institutions. (When asked by a reporter whether he

planned to form a city government for his eponymous model community, George Pullman stated his

intentions clearly: “As long as the town of Pullman is owned by one association, there's little necessity

of agitating the subject of its control.”) That is to say: the historical company town was not, as a formal

matter of law, a “town” at all. And when they did operate as such, populated central cities could easily

swallow their enclaves through annexation—as Chicago did in 1889, when it annexed Pullman’s

company town into its borders (overcoming Pullman’s elaborate efforts to block the merger). This

possibility ended when states reformed their annexation laws during the first half of the twentieth

century to defer to “local” preferences—giving tiny corporate enclaves (like Starbase) an effective veto

over the annexation efforts of their central cities.

These developments occurred after the early socialists developed their home rule platform.

When early socialists were fighting for the delegation of unfettered policymaking authority to

municipalities, they could be reasonably confident that municipal officials—however vulnerable they

might be, as individuals, to corporate influence through the mechanisms of graft, bribery, and cultural

capture—would represent large and inclusive electorates (rather than the hollow shells that

contemporary enclaves often resemble). But amid today’s extreme jurisdictional fragmentation, efforts

to protect the legal authority of cities—if pursued without accounting for, or directly responding to,

these recent developments—risk ultimately facilitating this new strategy for corporate domination.

## Chapter 1: Regulating Location Incentives

In recent years, a growing share of state and local budgetary resources has been diverted to a small number of firms through multibillion-dollar location incentive megadeals, as represented by Amazon’s HQ2 search and Wisconsin’s Foxconn boondoggle. These companies have become adept at devising new mechanisms for extracting the public resources of local communities to secure a competition advantage over their market rivals. But legal scholarship has not considered the possibility that dominant firms’ incentive demands might implicate the statutory protections enacted to protect against unfair methods of competition and corporate dominance more broadly. This Article develops a historical, economic, and institutional case for using latent authority under the Federal Trade Commission Act to study the market consequences of inefficient incentive megadeals—and regulate certain anticompetitive practices that cause cognizable harms.

This Article uses location incentive megadeals to explore how federal regulation could help address a classic concern of state and local governance: structural corporate power over local communities. I demonstrate that the populist movement responsible for the enactment of our initial antimonopoly protections was substantially motivated by opposition to the lavish incentives demanded by private railroad companies, from competing towns, during the late nineteenth century. When Congress later strengthened those protections by creating the Federal Trade Commission in 1914, legislators were addressing harms understood to be created by unregulated interstate competition for mobile corporate tax location. Reviewing recent reporting and empirical findings, this Article suggests that contemporary megadeals create harms directly analogous to those of concern to past legislative drafters: to healthy product competition; to consumers of private and public goods; to labor market structure; and to democratic self-governance. Finally, this Article argues that federal market supervision offers various institutional advantages as compared to previous (unsuccessful) attempts to rein in this source of public resource misallocation—accommodating key policy considerations and overcoming the coordination challenges that prevent localities from acting on their own.

II.  STRUCTURAL POWER IN THE MARKET FOR CORPORATE INVESTMENT

This historical context informs the case for conceptualizing location incentives as being within

the proper scope of competition policy. This Part uses contemporary incentive megadeals to illustrate

how corporate power—conceptualized as structural in nature—affects the interjurisdictional “market”

for mobile corporate investment. Economists conceptualize location incentives as reflecting the

market-clearing price for private capital, established through a process of competitive bidding from

local jurisdictions. Reviewing recent empirical studies, this Part shows that the best available evidence

suggests that structural power distorts the interjurisdictional bidding market for mobile economic

activity. This form of market power helps explain the robust relationship researchers have established

between firm size and the receipt of generous—and economically unjustified—location incentives.

A. Antimonopoly Concerns About Structural Power

During the Gilded Age and Progressive Era, contemporary reformers concluded that the

dominant firms had attained a destructive and undemocratic power over local communities. Writing

in 1879, Henry George used the railroads’ subsidy demands—made of competing towns—to illustrate

the nature of this distinctive power:

But there is another far more insidious . . . form of monopoly. In the aggregation of large masses of capital under a common control there is developed a new and essentially different power . . . which, as aggregation proceeds, rises upon it is destructive. It is a power of the same kind as that which [King] James [I] granted to Buckingham, and it is often exercised with as reckless a disregard . . . . For the threat of the railroad company is not merely to deprive the

town of the benefits which the railroad might give; it is to put it in a far worse position than if no railroad had been built.168

As K. Sabeel Rahman recounts, historical antimonopoly thought—and the political movements that

reformists supported—were centrally concerned with this form of power. Progressive Era reformers

observed that large corporations “had acquired a size and a degree of economic and political power

that could affect a wide range of other actors in society—not only [their] own workers, but also small

businesses, and governments threatened by competitive pressure and corporate inﬂuence.”169

Concern about the consequences of dominant firms’ structural power animated not only

antimonopoly thinking but also the legislative reforms described in Part I. Over subsequent decades,

comparative political economists have closely studied this form of power by private capital over public

governance—conceptualizing it as structural in nature. From a classic account:

This theory [of structural dependence] begins with the hypothesis that the entire society depends on the allocation of resources chosen by owners of capital. Investment decisions have public and long-lasting consequences: they determine the future possibilities of production, employment, and consumption for all. Yet they are private decisions. . . . [B]ecause the entire society depends on the owners of capital, so must the state. Whether particular governments have interests and goals of their own or they act on behalf of a coalition of groups or a class, the pursuit of any objectives that require material resources places governments in the situation of structural dependence.170

More recent scholarship has emphasized that firms’ structural power is contingent on the mobility of

private assets in their control as well as the level of jurisdictional fragmentation within the relevant

market. As Jacob Hacker and Paul Pierson observe, firms’ structural power is particularly heightened

As these brief reviews demonstrate, the legal and political strategies currently imagined to be

available as a check against this form of corporate dominance have fallen short for three general

The two available state-led solutions both have been hindered by the same prisoners’ dilemma

that also prevented effective action against either the railroad subsidies of the late nineteenth century

D. A Regulatory Approach Consistent with Congressional Design

This Article contends that regulatory scrutiny of location incentive megadeals—and corporate

dominance over local communities more broadly—can take a wide variety of forms that are not

limited by judicial immunity doctrines. In addition to the features that allow the FTC to exercise unique

regulatory authority over certain categories of anticompetitive state and local policy, other aspects of

the agency’s institutional design make it particularly well-positioned to fulfill this proposed role.

This observation begins with the FTC’s intended role as expert agency with broad investigative

and rulemaking authority. As Neil Averitt notes, the FTC “has special characteristics that suit it to the

exercise of a broader authority than a district court would have.”366 Significantly, the FTC’s leadership

has “developed expertise in the fields of business, law, and economics, and, in addition, [has] the

assistance of a staff of industrial organization economists.”367 Even short of new rulemaking or

enforcement actions under § 5, the FTC also is specifically empowered under § 6 with the ability to

require an entity to file “annual and special . . . reports or answers in writing to specific questions” and

to provide information about the entity’s “organization, business, conduct, practices, management,

and relation to other corporations, partnerships, and individuals.”368 Additionally, § 6 allows the FTC

“[t]o make public from time to time” portions of the information that it obtains, where disclosure

would serve the public interest.369

## CONCLUSION

To date, legal scholarship has tended to conceptualize corporate location incentives as misguided

local tax policy: wasteful, but not unlawful; tax policy, rather than part of an antimonopoly regulatory

agenda; a local rather than national concern. This Article challenges each aspect of this consensus. It

reframes inefficient location incentive megadeals as resulting from the exercise of structural corporate

power in the interjurisdictional market for corporate investment (rather than misguided lawmaking

alone). This Article draws from history to show that landmark antimonopoly legislation was enacted

in response to concerns about competition harms that had resulted from the unregulated competition

for mobile corporate capital. It charts a path forward for federal supervision—administered under the

legal authorities of the FTC Act, but implemented as market regulation. Finally, it demonstrates that

the general goal of protecting against unfair and anticompetitive business practices related to firms’

incentive demands could be pursued through a variety of actions—ranging from governmental studies

and routine information requests to more ambitious options including new rulemaking and

enforcement actions. Most broadly, this Article uses corporate location incentive megadeals as a case

study to demonstrate that structural corporate dominance over local communities is a problem that

federal regulation can help address.

## Chapter 2: Anti-Oligarchy State Constitutions

This Article describes how populist reform movements during the Gilded Age and Progressive Era used state constitutions to mitigate the democratic harms of concentrated wealth. It explores how a coalition of Western and Prairie state reformers—indebted farmers, militant miners, and rural  socialists—reﬁned a theory of state constitutionalism over three decades of eﬀorts to challenge railroad capitalism. Through archival research about conditions preceding the 1907 Oklahoma and 1910 Arizona statehood conventions, I show that key institutional design choices were motivated by a shared commitment against concentrated economic power. In particular, two features of state constitutions that are commonly observed to distinguish them from the federal charter—their considerable length and detail, and the availability of formal amendment—were intended (in these new states) to facilitate democratization from oligarchy. These distinctive features are viewed by some scholars today as constitutional defects: unwise and unwarranted departures from the celebrated static minimalism of our national charter. Such criticisms echo the reception that initially met these episodes of agrarian constitution-tinkering from Eastern elites, who widely derided the Oklahoma and Arizona charters as “freak” documents undeserving of constitutional status. But these design choices—intentional and considered rejections of court-interpreted constitutional generality—were innovated to overcome a particular form of authoritarianism (entrenched oligarchy) that undermined democratic self-governance. This state-level experimentation, in turn, contributed to national debates about the nature of a constitution and the material stakes of its design. I trace an overlooked history documenting how reformers, and their opponents, learned from these state conﬂicts—shaping their thinking not only about state constitutions, but about constitutionalism.

## CONCLUSION

How diﬀicult should it be to formally amend the text of a written constitution? What role should

popular majorities have in this process—and what level of consensus should be required from them

to establish higher law? Once drafted, who should have ﬁnal authority over its interpreted meaning?

Should a constitutional text ever speak directly (as through elaborate “statutory” detail) to timely

questions of evolving public interest, like abortion access or workers’ compensation? Or does the

nature of a fundamental charter require that drafters provide only broad generalities, to be later applied

to speciﬁc situations by judges? Should their decisions—or those judges—be subject to any form of

public revision or recall?

Generations of legal academics have debated these (most basic) questions of constitutionalism—

typically, in American scholarship over the past century, by evaluating the federal model of court-

centered static minimalism. Describing our state constitutions’ distinctive design, many academic

commentaries conceptualize them as a counterweight to the unamendable countermajoritarianism of

our federal charter.361 Indeed, some commentaries characterize this diﬀerence as a normatively

desirable feature of our federalism design. Jeﬀery Sutton, for example, has remarked: “Time has

conﬁrmed the virtues of having a Madisonian federal charter that’s diﬀicult to amend and ﬁfty

Jeﬀersonian state charters that are easier for each generation to amend.”362

As a descriptive matter, this structural departure between the models of constitutionalism that

dominate at diﬀerent vertical levels of our federal system is inarguable. But this history demonstrates

that some of the most notable departures from the federal model were not intended to operate as a

## Chapter 3: Governing The Company Town

This Article explores the forms of public and private governance that facilitate localized corporate domination. Researchers have documented the oppressive employment relationship that characterized historical “company towns,” but few accounts yet have examined these communities as local governments. I use archival research to identify institutional continuities between corporate ﬁefdoms like George Pullman’s model town outside Chicago (1880-1898) and Disney’s self-governed district near Orlando (1967-2023). I demonstrate that local government law has contributed to the recent reemergence of company-dominated enclaves, namely by deferring to private governance and facilitating jurisdictional fragmentation. During the Gilded Age and Progressive Era, proprietors of company-owned towns exercised absolute control over workers through the private law of property and contract. Mining bosses and industrial barons like Pullman intentionally rejected the municipal form, using dismissal and eviction to enforce company policy as the operative governing authority within their dominions. This strategy became less eﬀective after the New Deal, leading observers to pronounce the demise of the company town. But I argue that parallel developments in local government law have allowed the company town’s continuation through new institutional forms, enabling corporate titans to wield public powers without accountability to any broad public. Rather than facilitating domination over captive worker-residents, these institutional forms are used primarily to externalize costs and escape democratic obligations like taxation—goals that also deeply shaped the governance of historical company towns. I review this playbook through several recent case studies, demonstrating how territorial and functional fragmentation have facilitated the proliferation of corporate enclaves—allowing spatiallyconcentrated private capital to secede from local democratic control. I suggest that the company town can be understood as a democratic phenomenon: a distinctive form of private tyranny. Since the Founding, theorists have acknowledged the vulnerability of small and non-diverse jurisdictions to tyrannical rule-by-faction. By contextualizing new examples like Elon Musk’s eﬀorts to incorporate his model towns in Texas, I show that this fear is realized where corporate interests either commandeer our formal institutions of governance or displace their typical role in structuring public life.

The company town manifests tyrannical faction rule

How should we understand the nature of this democratic phenomenon, and where should we

expect to observe it? I suggest that the company town represents a pure manifestation of the classic

concern in American political thought—articulated by James Madison, particularly in The Federalist

papers 10 and 47151—about the “tyranny” that accompanies domination of faction within a given

jurisdiction. According to Madison, “the very deﬁnition of tyranny” is “[t]he accumulation of all

powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands.”152 In particular, this fear is thought to

be realized when such powers are accumulated to some “faction” that can wield them against others,

or against the interests of the larger polity, without democratic restraint.153 The company town, in this

understanding, represents an antidemocratic concentration of governing authority to a single group

whose interests are adverse to the rights of others.

In Madison’s phrasing, a faction is deﬁned not by its numerosity but rather by the nature of the

governing interest that unites the group: the quality of being adverse to the rights of others or the

community as whole.154 One way to understand the democratic harm presented by the company town

is as validation of Madison’s fear: the unrestrained rule of faction within its own jurisdiction.155

What insights are gained from conceptualizing the company town as a democratic phenomenon?

Implicit in Madison’s account—his identiﬁcation of the two ways that faction could be prevented—

is an argument about the diﬀerent pathways by which faction could maintain absolute (tyrannical)

manipulation of boundaries will provide an opportunity for faction to dominate governance of

fragmented jurisdictions even where electoral democracy is operative within them.

Avoiding democracy by governing through private law

Community life in the historical company town was strictly regulated. Restrictive codes of conduct

mandated adherence to employer-imposed morality codes and restrictions on private political

speech—all enforced through community surveillance.177 These industrial communities were not

governments, but they were governed: The actions, and even thoughts, of worker-residents were

tightly controlled by their employers. Within the domain of its fully-owned territory, one account

observed, “The company alone was the town legislative and executive body. It handed down all rules

and regulations and was responsible for putting them into eﬀect.”178

Proﬁling company towns in the Appalachian South, Robert Eller documents how “power of the

mine operator” extended “over almost every facet of village aﬀairs”:

Limitations of private law and the allure of the public form

For the subset of company goals that could be achieved by exercising control over captive worker-

residents, this displacement strategy—governing through private law, backed by public enforcement,

within fully-owned territorial domains—proved highly eﬀective for some time. The federal

preemption of particular rights of property and contract, especially the right to dismiss (and evict)

workers for forming a union, in combination with parallel changes in economic geography, eventually

would change the strategic calculus that had for so long motivated companies’ rejection of the

municipal form.212 But even before the New Deal, town bosses seeking to govern through private law

saw the limitations of their strategy—and the early allure of public powers.213 Although consolidated

property ownership provided the primary mechanism by which governance by minority faction was

achieved during this period, there remained certain state functions that could not be privatized. For

minoritarian control of those public powers, two other strategies emerged: 1) ﬁscal cost-shifting to

the ﬁrm, exchanging payment for control, and 2) democratic suppression and public corruption.

Shrinking the sphere: domination through concentration

Madison warned that any “faction”—of any size, including a single corporation or wealthy

patron—can evade democratic accountability by self-governing, as unchallenged majority, within its

own fragmented domain.247 Where powerful incumbents control the adjustment (or strategic non-

adjustment) of jurisdictional boundaries, their lack of numerosity is no obstacle to the attainment of

public governing authority. It was through this playbook that the Pitt family represented the notorious

Old Sarum pocket borough without democratic challenge: as nominated by “popular” majority among

its seven fully-owned burgages.248 Through jurisdictional fragmentation, any minoritarian faction can

thus become a “majority”—not by popular persuasion, but through strategic (re)deﬁnition of the

whole.

Drawing from Madison’s institutional analysis, let us stipulate that tyrannical rule by faction

requires three components—all of which are regulated, in the United States, by local government law.

First, its members or beneﬁciaries must be able to sort across territorial space, namely by excluding

from the electorate any who might challenge their interests. As a historical matter, this is typically

achieved through concentrated land ownership (as in the pocket boroughs).249 Second, faction—once

neatly sorted—must be able to exit, jurisdictionally, from the larger and more diverse democratic

whole.250 The initial establishment of faction rule requires only these two components. But even after

Writing in 2019 about the “constitutional problem” presented by small states with non-diverse

economies, David Schleicher observed that “Vermont could theoretically suﬀer the same fate as

former British pocket boroughs like Old Sarum.”299 As he noted, an interest group “can be quite small

contemporary pocket boroughs—the legally-protected use of public power, attained by faction

through its control over a sparsely-populated (“rotten”) jurisdiction—is even more pronounced at the

local level, manifested in institutional form as the corporate enclave.

The distinctive harms of the incorporated company town

These foregoing examples represent the “pure case” corporate enclave: contemporary pocket

boroughs, governed by spatially-consolidated capital as unencumbered by internal democratic

constraint. This strategy can be observed today also in the ongoing eﬀort by Elon Musk to incorporate

distinctive outliers—illustrating the danger of abuse under current law, in the absence of meaningful

constraints.338

We should expect that these various forms of eﬀective secession will remain attractive to ﬁrms

seeking market advantage for as long as they remain eﬀective vehicles for escaping democratic

regulation, evading shared obligations like taxation, and accessing the powers of public authority.

## CONCLUSION

Writing decades before the Massachusetts legislature chartered the textile town of Lowell, Madison

predicted a relationship between the degree of jurisdictional fragmentation within a polity and the

danger of tyrannical faction within each. This danger can be mitigated, he suggests, through the

strategic adjustment of jurisdictional boundaries to ensure that the electorate is numerous and diverse

in its interests. Madison predicted that the tyranny of faction rule would be more likely to emerge in a

fragmented polity, where small groups with aligned interests (that are opposed to the public) have the

ability to self-govern without opposition in private ﬁefdoms.

His concern has direct implications for the body of public law that directly governs jurisdictional

fragmentation and the allocation of governing authority across vertical levels of government of

diﬀerent size. The past century of developments in local government law has helped facilitate the

preservation of the historical corporate enclave across new forms. Yesterday’s employer-owned

communities oﬀer a necessary reference point to understand the public values implicated in the law

that governs the boundaries and powers of local governments. History demonstrates that localized

corporate domination is contingent on our institutional design—helping to reveal a path not taken.

Rather than attending rarely, indirectly, and only belatedly to the downstream consequences of

corporate ﬁefdoms, our public law should directly prevent their emergence.

## Chapter 4: Tax Base Fragmentation as a Dimension of Metropolitan Inequality

The United States devolves responsibility for providing critical services to local governments. With limited centralized transfers, the ability to provide these services is largely determined by the base of taxable wealth that is contained within contested municipal boundaries. We document how jurisdictional fragmentation and economic segregation interact to create tax base fragmentation, the unequal allocation of taxable property wealth across jurisdictional boundaries. The level of tax base fragmentation varies across the country, but is substantial in many large metros, and is associated with both the amount and type of revenue raised by local governments. We also identify hundreds of individual jurisdictions that disproportionately beneﬁt from or are harmed by tax base fragmentation, showing how the institutional structure of US ﬁscal federalism allows some jurisdictions to function as tax shelters for wealthy residents and corporations, while conversely subjecting other jurisdictions to severe ﬁscal stress, even in broadly prosperous metropolitan areas.

I. INTRODUCTION

In the United States, local governments are primarily responsible for funding a wide range of

essential public services, including primary and secondary education, public safety, and local

infrastructure. The level of spending on these services has been linked to residents’ life outcomes in

domains from economic mobility to health to education (e.g. Lobao et al., 2012; McCullough & Leider,

2016; O’Brien et al., 2025; Rauscher & Shen, 2022).

In performing this role, local jurisdictions in the United States operate under legal and ﬁscal

constraints that are atypical among high-income countries. Localities in the United States receive no

unconditional funding from the federal government (Weir & King, 2021). To fund local services like

education, infrastructure, and public safety, they must generate a large share of their revenue from the


<!-- Page 294 -->


286

taxable wealth and economic activity that exists within their own boundaries, primarily from property

taxes and user charges. At the same time, comparatively permissive municipal incorporation laws have

resulted in a proliferation of local governments—fragmenting across separate jurisdictions not only

political authority, but also the base of taxable wealth and economic activity (Freemark et al., 2020).

The combination of these ﬁscal arrangements is distinctive: even other federal political systems

generally achieve much higher levels of interjurisdictional redistribution through ﬁscal transfers

centralized at the national or regional level (Béland & Lecours, 2014; McCabe, 2019; Stark, 2009).

Under the U.S. institutional design, local government policy—both the services provided and the level

of taxation—can vary enormously over distances of just a few miles.

A growing interdisciplinary literature has described how jurisdictional fragmentation, local

revenue generation, and residential segregation interact to create stark ﬁscal disparities between

jurisdictions within the same metropolitan area (Freemark et al., 2020; Pacewicz & Robinson, 2021;

Trounstine, 2018, 2021; Weir & King, 2021). But although widely acknowledged, researchers have

lacked a precise conceptual framework for this interjurisdictional ﬁscal inequality, and it has not been

directly measured at scale: most quantitative studies have examined economic segregation or

jurisdictional fragmentation in isolation, without capturing how these phenomena interact to limit the

own-source ﬁscal capacity of local jurisdictions. Research that directly considers ﬁscal capacity has

predominantly taken the form of case studies, due in part to institutional variation across states (e.g.

Pacewicz & Robinson, 2021).

In this paper we introduce a methodology for measuring tax base fragmentation: the unequal

distribution of taxable wealth across political jurisdictions within a deﬁned geographic territory. As a

dimension of metropolitan inequality, tax base fragmentation is distinct from commonly studied

phenomena like economic segregation and jurisdictional fragmentation; as a ﬁscal constraint on local

governments, it operates in parallel to legal constraints such as tax and expenditure limitations (TELs;


<!-- Page 295 -->


287

Martin, 2008) or regional economic decline. Our approach directly quantiﬁes the extent to which the

territorial boundaries of local governments overlap onto spatial patterns of economic segregation to

create interjurisdictional ﬁscal inequalities within U.S. metropolitan areas.

We measure tax base fragmentation using a dataset of 138 million geocoded property tax

records, covering approximately 96 percent of the U.S. population. We ﬁrst calculate the per capita

appraised real property wealth for each general-purpose local jurisdiction and public school district in

the country, allowing direct comparison of the ﬁscal resources available to municipalities, counties,

and school districts around the country. While many studies have deployed indirect proxies of ﬁscal

capacity like neighborhood-level income or collected revenues, our dataset precisely measures the

own-source ﬁscal resources that are available to local governments from the taxation of real property

within their jurisdictional boundaries, independent of legal constraints and political decisions about

how to tax that assessed wealth.

We then create a metric, the tax base fragmentation quotient (TFQ), that measures the share

of each metropolitan area’s total property tax base that would need to shift across local jurisdictional

borders in order for all municipalities within the metropolitan area to have the same tax base per

capita—or, alternatively, the amount of ﬁscal equalization that would be required to equalize ﬁscal

capacity.

The level of tax base fragmentation varies widely across U.S. metropolitan areas. In nine

metros (largely agricultural and resort communities), more than half of all taxable property wealth

would have to change jurisdictions to create per capita equality. Among larger metros, more than a

ﬁfth of all property wealth in Bridgeport, Connecticut, Detroit, Michigan, or Miami, Florida, would

have to shift across jurisdictional boundaries to achieve this result. The other end of the spectrum is

represented by Hawai’i, which has no local governments below its ﬁve counties. Despite high levels

of spatial economic segregation within the Honolulu metro, all taxable property wealth is located


<!-- Page 296 -->


288

within one jurisdiction—Honolulu County—and all residents share the same local tax base. We

demonstrate empirically that tax base fragmentation is only weakly correlated with economic

segregation and jurisdictional fragmentation; it represents a distinct dimension of variation across U.S.

metro areas.

Our measures also allow us to identify individual municipalities that disproportionately beneﬁt

from, or are harmed by, tax base fragmentation. We document the existence of more than 500

“municipal tax havens,” independent jurisdictions with per capita tax bases many times larger than

their metropolitan average. These include nationally known bastions of residential aﬀluence like

Malibu, California, or Miami Beach, Florida, as well as locally prestigious suburbs such as the Park

Cities in Dallas or Bloomﬁeld Hills, Michigan. But in addition to these well-known examples, we

identify hundreds of smaller and less famous jurisdictions—including numerous corporate enclaves

with virtually no residents but millions (or even billions) of dollars’ worth of commercial property.

These jurisdictions eﬀectively function as tax shelters for their residents and corporations, allowing

access to the broader metropolitan economy and providing locally-exclusive services without

contributing to programs that beneﬁt neighboring jurisdictions. Our unique data sources and

methodology allows us to deﬁnitively identify these jurisdictions across the entire United States—and

precisely quantify the degree to which their advantageous ﬁscal positions result from tax base

fragmentation—for the ﬁrst time.

On the other end of the economic spectrum, we identify a distinctive type of ﬁscal need that

operates separately from other forms of place-based disadvantage: jurisdictions whose per-capita tax

base is only a small fraction of the average of their broader metropolitan area. These “ﬁscally

impoverished jurisdictions” (c.f. O’Brien and Schechtl 2024) are not simply poor places (although most

are), but rather municipalities that are jurisdictionally excluded from accessing the taxable wealth of

their metropolitan area.


<!-- Page 297 -->


289

We conclude our analysis by showing how these identiﬁed divergences in local ﬁscal capacity

translate into enacted ﬁscal policy. Linking our measure of jurisdictional property wealth to municipal

revenue data from the U.S. Census of Governments, we ﬁnd that resource-poor municipalities source

a greater percentage of their budgets from intergovernmental transfers, user charges, ﬁnes, and

forfeitures, as compared to other municipalities in their same state and metropolitan area. Our results

provide suggestive evidence that tax base fragmentation may contribute to localities’ reliance on

extractive methods of revenue generation (Henricks & Harvey, 2017; Pacewicz & Robinson, 2021).

We also examine whether interjurisdictional diﬀerences in own-source property wealth are fully oﬀset

by these alternative sources of revenue or intergovernmental transfers (as would be the case under full

ﬁscal centralization), and ﬁnd that they are not. On average, a 1 percent increase in tax base per capita

is associated with a 0.25 percent increase in total revenue from all sources, compared to other

municipalities in the same state and metro. This result suggests that tax base fragmentation

meaningfully shapes local public spending: while tax base-poor jurisdictions partially compensate by

turning to other revenue sources or taxing local property wealth at higher rates, this is not suﬀicient

to compensate for their lower levels of own-source ﬁscal resources.

Tax base fragmentation is one of many distinct pathways through which ﬁscal divergence

between jurisdictions is created; it operates in parallel to the many other dimensions of metropolitan

inequality that characterize the United States political economy. But our ﬁndings provide evidence

that tax base fragmentation is not only distinctive from other well-studied phenomena—including

spatial segregation, jurisdictional fragmentation, regional disinvestment, and legal constraints on local

revenue authority—but also helps explain divergent outcomes that are of broad interest to researchers.

By conceptualizing and measuring this mechanism of spatial inequality, we contribute a more precise

understanding of the ways that local government fragmentation and economic segregation interact to

create ﬁscal constraint. While our analysis here focuses on the sources and amounts of local revenue,

290

we conclude the article by identifying, as an agenda for future research, numerous other outcomes

that might be explained in part by tax base fragmentation.

II. LOCAL GOVERNMENTS AND FISCAL DECENTRALIZATION IN THE UNITED STATES

In the United States, local governments are the primary providers of K-12 education, public

safety, sanitation services, and certain categories of infrastructure. They collectively accounted for

almost $2 trillion of spending in 2017, close to one-fourth of all governmental spending in that year

(US Census Bureau, 2024). This spending has been shown to impact residents’ life outcomes across a

variety of domains. For instance, McCullough and Leider (2016) ﬁnd that counties with higher levels

of local government spending across a range of health and non-health domains had better public

health outcomes. O’Brien et al. (2025) show that metros where local spending was more centralized

(i.e. a greater portion occurred at the state or county level) had less spatial variation in the upward

mobility of low-income children, as would be expected if spending were beneﬁcial for upward

mobility. Lobao et al. (2012) show that counties with greater governmental capacity had lower poverty

rates among residents. Research on the consequences of school funding reforms that allocated greater

state funding to poorer districts has generally found that increased spending led to improved

educational outcomes for children (Biasi, 2023; C. K. Jackson et al., 2016; Rauscher & Shen, 2022).

Compared to other countries, local governments in the United States are highly fragmented:

The U.S. has roughly 90,000 independent jurisdictions, ranging from counties to cities to towns to

independent school districts to special purpose governments like business improvement districts and

water and sewer authorities. Local government law has contributed to this jurisdictional proliferation

by facilitating municipal incorporation and hindering annexation (Briﬀault, 1990; K. T. Jackson, 1987).

Both historically and in the present, racial antagonism has been a central driver of local government

fragmentation, as white residents depart diverse cities and use incorporation and zoning law to create


<!-- Page 299 -->


291

new municipalities that will not have to share space, funding, or services with poorer residents of color

(Godinez Puig, 2024; Kahrl, 2024; Trounstine, 2021; Zhang, 2024).

This fragmentation has important ﬁscal consequences because the U.S. does comparatively

little to ameliorate ﬁscal disparities between localities. Most other federal systems characterized by

political and programmatic decentralization feature considerably higher inter-jurisdictional

redistribution through ﬁscal transfers centralized at the national or regional level (Béland & Lecours,

2014; Freemark et al., 2020; McCabe, 2019; Weir & King, 2021). But in the U.S., local governments

must generate a large fraction—almost two-thirds in 2017 (US Census Bureau, 2024)—of their

revenue from taxes and fees levied on the economic resources that exist within their boundaries. One

consequence of this design is that in the United States, much more than in other countries, political

fragmentation—through the proliferation of local governments—is associated with divergence in

local ﬁscal capacity—via the fragmentation of ﬁscal units that contain varying amounts of taxable wealth

(Highsmith, 2019; see Bradlow, 2021 for discussion of a similar phenomenon in South Africa).

Although this aspect of metropolitan governance distinguishes the United States as a whole,

the various features that interact to create these jurisdictional inequalities are each characterized by

substantial variation within the country. Diﬀerences in state law and quirks of history mean that some

metropolitan areas are much more politically fragmented than others.  Diﬀerences in other state-level

policies mediate the relationship between local governments’ own-source ﬁscal capacity and their

ability to provide essential public services. States delegate to localities the legal authority to generate

revenue through taxation of real property within their jurisdictional boundaries (Scharﬀ, 2016).

Particularly since the 1970s, many have imposed tax and expenditure limitations (TELs) that directly

limit the total revenue local governments are allowed to raise, the tax rates they can charge, or the

rates at which property assessments can increase (Martin, 2008; Mullins, 2010). One result of these

limitations has been a shift towards user fees and other forms of non-tax revenue (e.g. Joyce & Mullins,


<!-- Page 300 -->


292

1991; Skidmore, 1999; Henricks & Harvey, 2017). And although roughly one-third of all local revenue

is distributed from higher levels of government (US Census Bureau, 2024), states and counties also

vary widely in the degree and forms of transfers they provide to their local governments—and the

extent to which they centralize service provision at the state or county level, or distribute it among

many municipalities or special purpose districts. As O’Brien et al. (2025) describe, these diﬀerences

often reﬂect idiosyncratic processes of historical development rather than contemporary politics or

redistribution-motivated eﬀorts to equalize ﬁscal capacity.

III. CONCEPTUALIZING TAX BASE FRAGMENTATION

This paper seeks to document tax base fragmentation as a distinct dimension of metropolitan

inequality. We conceptualize tax base fragmentation as the inequality in own-source ﬁscal capacity

between local jurisdictions within a given region that is created by interactions between economic

segregation and jurisdictional fragmentation. When the tax base of a metropolitan area is highly

fragmented, the own-source ﬁscal capacity of speciﬁc jurisdictions within it will diverge widely. Even

in broadly prosperous metro areas, particular jurisdictions may face persistent ﬁscal shortfalls; even in

struggling regions, speciﬁc municipalities may continue to access well-funded local public goods.

Both economic segregation and jurisdictional fragmentation have been extensively studied in

recent decades, though generally as separate phenomena. Social scientists have developed various

metrics to capture aspects of both concepts—each of which has been hypothesized as being causally

connected to public service provision (e.g. Hendrick et al., 2011; Trounstine, 2016, 2018). In this

section, we brieﬂy review some of these measures, highlighting how each is conceptually distinct from

the variation that we seek to quantify: the fragmentation of taxable wealth (rather than, for example,

land or residents) across jurisdictional boundaries (rather than neighborhoods or statistical units) within a

metropolitan area. We also show how tax base fragmentation more directly tracks the mechanisms

through which segregation and fragmentation are theorized to shape own-source local ﬁscal capacity.


<!-- Page 301 -->


293

Residential segregation

A substantial body of evidence demonstrates that when residents of the same city live in

segregated neighborhoods, they are less willing to fund collective goods (Fischel, 2002; Trounstine,

2016). Racial residential segregation has been most commonly measured by the dissimilarity index,

which measures the extent to which the population of each sub-area within a metro diﬀers in racial

composition from the metro as a whole, and the isolation index, which measures the extent to which

members of a particular racial group live in neighborhoods populated by other members of their group

(Massey & Denton, 1988). Economic segregation—the extent to which people of diﬀerent income or

wealth levels live near one another—is most commonly measured through the rank-order information

theory index (Reardon & Bischoﬀ, 2011).

Residential economic segregation is directly related to our concept of tax base fragmentation,

but they are distinct. When residents are separated not only by geographic distance but also by political

jurisdiction, the task of redistribution between segregated groups is not feasible through locally-funded

programs. This limitation operates not through voter preferences for public goods, but rather through

institutional constraints on own-source ﬁscal capacity. The stylized metropolitan areas depicted in Figure

4.1 illustrate this distinction. In the ﬁgure, the four metros contain identical amounts of total wealth

(with residents visually represented as numbers that correspond to their property wealth). Metros A

and B diﬀer in their level of economic segregation: Metro A is relatively integrated, with rich and poor

households living in close proximity, while Metro B shows stark economic segregation. But because

all residents of each territory live in just one ﬁscal unit, there is no diﬀerence between Metros A and

B in ﬁscal capacity, deﬁned as per capita property wealth.

of jurisdictional fragmentation focus on the number and responsibilities of local governments, rather than

The literature on jurisdictional fragmentation makes two important conceptual distinctions:

between fragmentation and concentration, and between horizontal and vertical fragmentation (Boyne,

1992). Fragmentation measures aim to capture the number of distinct governmental units, while

concentration measures capture “market shares or the distribution of the responsibilities of local

public-sector entities.” (Hendrick et al., 2011, p. 478). With respect to ﬁscal capacity, the consequences

of a given level of tax base fragmentation will depend on the degree to which spending authority is

concentrated at a particular level and type of government.

Horizontal fragmentation refers to “the number of units within the same tier of local

government (e.g., the number of municipalities in a particular area)” while vertical fragmentation refers

to “the number of tiers of local government” (Goodman, 2019, p. 135). Common measures include

the number of local governments per capita and the number of local governments per square mile

(Hendrick et al., 2011). But while these measures capture the fragmentation of government units, they

fail to capture the fragmentation of economic resources.

To see how this is true, compare Metros C and D in Figure 4.1. Both of these metropolitan

areas are fragmented into three independent municipalities and have the same amount of total taxable

wealth. But the lack of economic segregation in Metro C means that all municipalities have the same

per capita tax base, while in Metro D the ﬁscal capacity of the municipalities is highly unequal. Existing

measures of jurisdictional fragmentation would score both of these metropolitan areas as being

identically fragmented. In so doing, they would be accurately capturing something important—the

degree of political fragmentation—but they would miss the diﬀerences in own-source ﬁscal capacity

that result from the overlap of those boundaries onto spatial patterns of segregation. Just as the

segregation measures above fail to capture jurisdictional proliferation, the existing measures of


<!-- Page 304 -->


296

jurisdictional fragmentation fail to capture spatial segregation. Directly measuring how ﬁscal resources

are segmented across jurisdictions requires quantifying the interaction between these two phenomena.

IV. MEASURING TAX BASE FRAGMENTATION

We conceptualize tax base fragmentation as the unequal allocation of taxable real property

wealth across jurisdictional boundaries within a metropolitan area. To study this phenomenon we

introduce two measures. At the jurisdictional scale, we calculate the ﬁscal capacity ratio (FCR), which

measures the per capita resources available to each jurisdiction, relative to is metropolitan area. At the

metropolitan scale, we calculate the tax base fragmentation quotient (TFQ), which measures the extent to

which jurisdictional boundaries fragment the tax base of the metropolitan area as a whole.

While tax base fragmentation can be calculated within any spatial unit, we focus on

metropolitan areas. Economic geographers consider metropolitan areas—deﬁned as a core city or

cities and the surrounding areas from which they draw commuters—to be the fundamental spatial

units of economic geography (Glaeser & Gottlieb, 2009; Storper, 1997). The metro area is the scale at

which key economic processes, such as agglomeration economies and import replacement, take place

(Glaeser et al., 1992; Jacobs, 1969). Metros thus form cohesive economic units, where the success of

any one resident, business, or sector depends on that of the rest of the metro. By measuring the

divergence of local ﬁscal capacity within metropolitan areas, we isolate the eﬀects of metropolitan tax

base fragmentation from cross-regional diﬀerences in economic prosperity.

Jurisdictional scale: the fiscal capacity ratio (FCR)

We operationalize local governments’ own-source ﬁscal capacity as the per capita taxable

property wealth that exists within their jurisdictional boundaries: the sum of the appraised value of all

taxable property, divided by the population. Our primary analyses focus on the taxation of real

property, historically the largest single source of own-source revenue for local governments (in this

respect, our use of “ﬁscal capacity” throughout this paper should be understood as stylized shorthand).


<!-- Page 305 -->


297

We examine taxable property wealth—rather than collected revenue or spending—because

we seek to isolate the jurisdictional distribution of ﬁscal resources. Revenue and spending reﬂect a

combination of local ﬁscal capacity (our focus) and other factors including legal restrictions on local

tax authority and residents’ political preferences about tax rates and service provision. By isolating

interjurisdictional diﬀerences in own-source ﬁscal capacity, we hope to facilitate future study of the

independent eﬀects of these various factors. For the same reason, we also exclude from our primary

measures all intergovernmental transfers—which can be used to overcome interjurisdictional diﬀerences

in ﬁscal capacity, but operate independently of tax base fragmentation.

To distinguish the eﬀect of tax base fragmentation from that of overall metropolitan wealth

or poverty, in most analyses we divide the per capita tax base of each jurisdiction by the (population-

weighted) average for its metropolitan area. This metric, which we term the “ﬁscal capacity ratio”

(FCR), quantiﬁes the degree to which each jurisdiction’s own-source ﬁscal capacity departs (in either

direction) from the overall average for its metropolitan region. It can be thought of as identifying the

“contribution” of every jurisdiction to the overall fragmentation of its metro’s combined base of

taxable real property. For municipality m in metropolitan area MSA, the ﬁscal capacity ratio is

calculated as:

V. DATA AND SPECIFICATION CHOICES

We analyze data on appraised real property values in 2019 from CoreLogic, a real estate data

company (CoreLogic, 2024). This dataset is compiled from publicly available assessor records, and

CoreLogic estimates that their data comprise over 99 percent of all taxable property parcels in the

United States, although geographic and value information is not available in all cases.

We use each parcel’s latitude and longitude to spatially join it to the census block, legal

jurisdiction, and metropolitan area in which it is located. We then undertake an extensive data cleaning

and validation process  to ensure that property value data is correct and comparable across states with

varying tax laws. The resulting ﬁnal dataset covers approximately 96 percent of the U.S. population

We augment the CoreLogic property data with 2020 Census population data from NHGIS (Manson

et al., 2017) and 2017 local and state government revenue data from the Census of Governments via

the Government Finance Database (Pierson et al., 2015; US Census Bureau, 2024).

Measuring taxable value

The starting point for a study of tax base fragmentation is a measure of the value of each

taxable property. Yet this is not a straightforward quantity to determine. The market value of a

property—what most people would consider the “true” value—constantly ﬂuctuates with consumer

preferences and economic conditions; it is directly observable only upon completed sale. Diﬀerent


<!-- Page 308 -->


300

states and jurisdictions adopt a wide range of techniques to produce an oﬀicial estimate of the value

of each taxable property, including those not recently sold. These techniques vary widely in their

accuracy (Kim et al., 2020), have documented systematic biases (Avenancio-León & Howard, 2022;

Berry, 2021) and have often been distorted for political ends, both in the past and recently (Kahrl,

2024; Martin, 2008; Meisel, 2025), although standards like the Uniform Standards of Professional

Appraisal Practice have been developed to address some of these challenges. Yet there is no way to

avoid applying some sort of approximation method to estimate the current value of parcels not sold

in a given year: even simply using the most recent sale price, as done in California since the 1978

passage of Proposition 13, is an approximation approach (and for long-held properties, a famously

inaccurate one).

The oﬀicial estimate of the market value is generally referred to as the “appraised value” or

“estimated market value” (we use the term “appraised value” throughout this paper). Once it has been

created, some states further modify it to arrive at the “assessed value” or “taxable value” upon which

taxes are levied. These modiﬁcations can include state-imposed limits on the rate at which the assessed

value can appreciate and exemptions that reduce the taxable amount. Additionally, several states assess

taxes on only a set fraction of each property’s appraised value. Michigan, for example, deﬁnes the

assessed value as 50 percent of the appraised value, while Illinois deﬁnes it as 33.33 percent of the

appraised value—except in Cook County, where it is 10 percent for most residential property and 25

percent for most other property (Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, 2023).  The tax bill is determined

by applying the local tax rate to the assessed value.

In our analysis, we take the appraised value as the object of study. This the oﬀicial estimate of

each property’s full market value—reﬂecting the approximation methods of the assessor, but not the

fractional assessment ratios, exemptions, and legal limitations on assessment that vary widely from

state to state. Appraised values can thus be meaningfully compared across state lines in a way that


<!-- Page 309 -->


301

assessed values cannot. Compared to the true market value, the appraised value reﬂects documented

systematic biases, generally overestimating the value of low-value properties and underestimating that

of high-value properties (Avenancio-León & Howard, 2022; Berry, 2021). But unlike market value, an

appraised value exists for all properties in each year.

More importantly, the appraised value better tracks the determinants of local ﬁscal

constraints—as visible to, and actually navigated by, local governments in the real world. The

appraised value is the result of a state legibility project: an oﬀicial government eﬀort to see the world,

so as to act upon it (Lee & Zhang, 2017; Scott, 1999). Like all such eﬀorts, it suﬀers from bias,

oversimpliﬁcation, and political interference. But these imperfections nonetheless shape how

governments understand their situation and what actions they take (de Souza Leão, 2022). The

documented inaccuracies of the appraisal process, which result in divergence from the “true” market

value, create real budgetary holes that impact municipal ﬁscal capacity (Berry, 2021; Kahrl, 2024). The

appraised values are, without question, less-than-perfect measures of the personal ﬁnancial situations

of individual homeowners. But for our purposes—understanding the (own-source) ﬁscal resources

that are available to local governments through the taxation of real property—they are arguably more

revealing than even a hypothetical, perfectly observed dataset of market value would be.

In our primary analysis, we include taxable real property of all types: residential, commercial,

industrial, agricultural, and vacant land, among others. Our goal is to enumerate the total value of all

taxable property within the boundaries of each jurisdiction: the base amount upon which policy

decisions about tax rates and spending are made (under the limitations imposed by state laws).

Geographic units

We examine tax base fragmentation across jurisdictional boundaries within metropolitan areas,

deﬁned as core-based statistical areas (CBSAs). CBSAs are groups of counties consisting of an urban

core of at least 10,000 residents and the surrounding areas from which it draws commuters.


<!-- Page 310 -->


302

Collectively, CBSAs contain roughly 310 million residents—approximately 94.5 percent of the U.S.

population in 2020. We use the 2020 CBSA delineations (Oﬀice of Management and Budget, 2021).

The U.S. system of local government is famously complex, with many layers of nested and

overlapping jurisdictions (Goodman, 2019; O’Brien et al., 2025).  In our primary analysis, we calculate

tax base fragmentation across general-purpose local governments: legally incorporated governments

with broadly deﬁned purposes and taxation authority, such as municipalities, counties, and towns.

General-purpose governments are typically the most salient form of local governments—residents are

more likely to know the mayor of their town than their district water commissioner—and they

collected 52 percent of all property tax revenue in 2017, more than all other types of local government

combined (US Census Bureau, 2024). We assign each parcel of property to the smallest general-

purpose local government containing it that has the independent power to raise property taxes:

generally the municipality or town for incorporated places and the county for unincorporated places.

Besides general-purpose local governments, school districts are the primary collectors of

property taxes in the United States, raising 40 percent of all property tax revenue in 2017. In many

metropolitan areas, school district boundaries closely follow those of general-purpose governments,

but they diverge markedly in some regions (notably including the South, as discussed below).

Appendix 3.1 shows results using school district rather than general-purpose government boundaries.

Another important form of local government in the United States is the special purpose district:

independent entities generally created for one particular purpose, such as sanitation or ﬁre protection.

Special districts are large in number and spatially overlap with other government types, but they collect

only 4 percent of property tax revenues (being far more dependent on fees and charges). For this

reason, as well as the lack of standardized data on district boundaries, we exclude these districts from

our analysis.

Our results show substantial variation in tax base fragmentation across U.S. metros. To

highlight the factors that contribute to this variation, we ﬁrst examine selected major metropolitan

Michigan; Honolulu, Hawaii; and Des Moines, Iowa (these three metropolitan areas also display the

according to their ﬁscal capacity ratio, with colored dots showing the spatial location of the highest-

and lowest-value 1 percent of properties (one dot per property).

Detroit, Michigan

Consider ﬁrst the Detroit-Warren-Dearborn Metropolitan Statistical Area, which ranks as the

most tax base-fragmented metropolitan area with over one million residents. Detroit has a TFQ of

0.235, indicating that 23.5 percent of the MSA’s total taxable property wealth would need to move

across jurisdictions to equalize their tax base per capita. Figure 4.2 maps the Detroit metro area.

The Detroit metropolitan area illustrates the underlying mechanisms of tax base

fragmentation. Detroit consistently ranks among the most racially segregated metro areas within the

United States: a 2011 study found that it ranked ﬁrst on both the dissimilarity and isolation indexes

(Logan & Stults, 2011). By our measure of neighborhood economic segregation, Detroit ranks third

among large metros—with a rank-order information theory index of 0.48, indicating that the observed

segregation of property value across tracts is 48 percent of its theoretical maximum.  But although

Detroit is highly segregated, it ranks near the middle in measures of jurisdictional fragmentation:

deploying a composite index of local government fragmentation, Hendrick and Shi (2015) found that

the Detroit metro area ranked 19th among the 51 largest metropolitan regions in the United States.

We identify 140 general-purpose local governments in the Detroit MSA, equating to 3.44 per 100,000

residents—60th among the 108 CBSAs with over 500,000 residents.


<!-- Page 313 -->


305

What stands out in the map of Detroit shown in Figure 4.2 is the way in which jurisdictional

fragmentation neatly overlaps onto spatial patterns of economic segregation to produce tax base

fragmentation. The purple dots show the locations of the 1 percent lowest-value properties in the

metropolitan area. Virtually all of them are found in Detroit proper, with a handful in suburban

Pontiac. Meanwhile, the highest-value 1 percent of properties (indicated by green dots), are found in

an entirely distinct set of suburban municipalities, with the exception of a small cluster in downtown

Detroit. As a result, the City of Detroit has a tax base of just $25,243 per capita, less than one-third

the metro-wide average of $82,354. This is indicated by its dark red shading, while several suburbs are

shown in dark blue, indicating per capita tax bases more than 500 percent of the metro average.

In 2013, the City of Detroit ﬁled for Chapter 9 municipal bankruptcy—the largest in U.S.

history. Accounts of Detroit’s debt crisis often emphasize region-wide patterns of economic decline

amid deindustrialization. But our measure documents that the City of Detroit occupies a uniquely

precarious ﬁscal position partly because of how jurisdictional boundaries segment metropolitan Detroit’s

property wealth—entirely independent of economic conditions facing the broader metropolitan area.

Honolulu, Hawaiʻi

In terms of tax base fragmentation, Honolulu occupies the opposite extreme from Detroit: its

TFQ is exactly 0, the minimum possible value. But that score does not reﬂect the absence of spatial

segregation. Like Detroit, the Honolulu metropolitan area is characterized by relatively pronounced

patterns of economic segregation: its rank-order information theory measure of 0.33 ranks 20th out

of 108 among large metros (if only residential properties are considered the Honolulu area ranks 15th,

with a value of 0.42). This is visible in the map shown in Figure 4.3, where the high-valued properties

are concentrated in downtown Honolulu and Waikiki, and low-valued properties are spread

throughout the rest of the island, especially its interior.


<!-- Page 314 -->

How, then, does Honolulu achieve the minimum possible score on our index of tax base

fragmentation? Through the complete absence of jurisdictional fragmentation. The state of Hawaiʻi

has no units of local government smaller than the county, meaning that the entire metropolitan area—

the entire island of Oʻahu—shares one tax base. For this reason, the pronounced spatial inequality in

Honolulu does not result in ﬁscal inequality between jurisdictions in the same way that comparable

spatial inequality does in Detroit. This distinction matters for the study of “place”: in metro areas like

Honolulu, whose jurisdictions include both poor and wealthy neighborhoods, even residents of

neighborhoods experiencing spatial or social disadvantage may nevertheless be able to access the sort

of well-funded public services that researchers have identiﬁed as potential mechanisms of place-based

opportunity.

Consequences of tax base fragmentation for individual jurisdictions

In addition to measuring the overall level of tax base fragmentation in every metropolitan area

in the United States, our analysis also provides new insights into the ﬁscal position of each jurisdiction

within them. Using the ﬁscal capacity ratio (FCR), we identify outlier jurisdictions whose ﬁscal capacity

is many times larger or smaller than their metropolitan average. While our metro-level results may be

intuitive to urban policy researchers, many of these outlier jurisdictions are quite small in terms of

both acreage and population—likely unfamiliar even to many local residents.

Consider again the case of metropolitan Detroit, shown in Figure 2. Numerous inﬂuential

studies of residential segregation and concentrated poverty have focused on the City of Detroit and

its major suburbs (e.g. Hartigan, 1999; Sugrue, 2014); it is perhaps not surprising that the region’s

overall level of tax base fragmentation is strikingly high. But our methodology identiﬁes speciﬁc

jurisdictions that stand out as even more pronounced ﬁscal outliers than the well-known examples of

Detroit proper and prominent wealthy suburbs like Grosse Pointe. The City of Inkster, shown in the

bottom center of the map, has a tax base of just $16,814 for each of its 25,126 residents—one-third

lower than Detroit itself. Meanwhile, Lake Angelus, the second-smallest city by population in the state,

had a tax base of over $700,000 per each of its 287 residents—more than twice as much as Grosse

Pointe Shores.

We ﬁnd that jurisdictions like Inkster and Lake Angelus exist in every region of the United

States, including in metropolitan areas characterized by comparatively low levels of overall

fragmentation. In this section we identify the speciﬁc municipalities that receive the greatest ﬁscal


<!-- Page 320 -->


312

advantage and disadvantage from tax base fragmentation within their metros, describing several

common patterns for each. We believe that these jurisdictions represent a distinctive form of place-

based advantage and disadvantage that merits greater attention from researchers and policymakers.

Municipal tax havens

Lake Angelus is an example of what we term a “municipal tax haven”: an independent general-

purpose local government whose boundaries contain enormous levels of property wealth relative to

neighboring jurisdictions. (Our use of this term highlights the institutional possibility for tax sheltering

that is provided through jurisdictional fragmentation; it is not intended to describe the historical

“motivation” behind the observed segmentation, which cannot be observed in our data.) For the

purposes of this section, we deﬁne municipal tax havens as jurisdictions whose taxable property wealth

per capita is at least three times the average for their metro area (an FCR above 300 percent). Although

any cutoﬀ point will be arbitrary in certain respects, we select 300 percent to highlight pronounced

outliers that may be of particular note to researchers and policymakers. Because we provide results

for every jurisdiction in our database, other researchers can create their own groupings or simply use

the FCR itself.

Using this criterion, we identify 501 distinct municipal tax havens, with a total combined

population of 1.8 million residents. Of 917 CBSAs, 184 have at least one municipal tax haven,

including 58 of the 108 metros with more than 500,000 residents. Among these jurisdictions are some

of the most famously wealthy municipalities in the country—Malibu, California; East Hampton, New

York; Palm Beach, Florida—as well as locally prestigious suburbs of many major cities, including

Cherry Hills Village, Colorado (outside Denver), Winnetka, Illinois (outside Chicago), and Highland

Park and University Park, Texas (completely surrounded by Dallas). But this list also includes dozens

of smaller and lesser-known residential suburbs, sometimes many times wealthier than the more

These jurisdictions represent a distinctive form of place-based disadvantage that deserves

greater scholarly attention. Unlike residents of a poor neighborhood that is located within a larger

municipality that also includes signiﬁcant ﬁscal resources (such as Brownsville, in the New York City
