social policy regimes, of “ﬁscal impoverishment”: the phenomenon where “some poor families are

made poorer still as a net result of the tax and transfer system” (Schechtl & O’Brien, 2024, p. 1250).

We describe here a parallel phenomenon—one that is unique to the comparatively distinctive US ﬁscal

regime—where jurisdictions are ﬁscally impoverished by the institutional design of local governance

within a region, rather than by metropolitan-level or region-wide economic trends.

These dynamics can be observed in Newark, New Jersey. Located less than 10 miles from Wall

Street, Newark’s boundaries contain a tax base of $49,050 per capita—less than one-third as much as

New York City, and less than one-tenth that of several nearby municipal tax havens. The city’s

metropolitan area, not region-wide economic diﬀiculties. In this respect, Newark and other ﬁscally

impoverished jurisdictions diﬀer from municipalities like Dayton or Youngstown, Ohio, whose facially

similar ﬁscal stresses derive from economic dislocations that have aﬀected their entire regions. In

some cases, such as Flint, Michigan, both processes are at work: the fragmented tax base of the metro

area has exacerbated the ﬁscal consequences of deindustrialization, leaving the city with a tax base of

less than $18,000 per resident.

By identifying jurisdictions whose boundaries align neatly with spatial patterns of segregation,

our methodology allows an alternative way of identifying the phenomenon of citywide poverty that

Michelle Wilde Anderson has argued represents “a speciﬁc and understudied pattern” of concentrated

deprivation (2022). While these municipalities may generate some revenue from sources other than

property taxes (including regressive alternatives like monetary sanctions and user fees), their lack of

suﬀicient property tax base leaves them in an extremely vulnerable ﬁnancial position: indeed, several

have gone through municipal bankruptcy in recent decades. Our analysis demonstrates that this ﬁscal

distress is not inevitable, nor even necessarily linked to deindustrialization or broad economic trends.

It reﬂects, at least in part, the U.S. ﬁscal system and the way it allows wealth to evade redistributive

local taxation.

VII. TAX BASE FRAGMENTATION AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT REVENUE

Thus far we have shown how municipal boundaries intersect with economic segregation to

fragment the tax base of most U.S. metros, creating substantial inequality in ﬁscal capacity between

nearby jurisdictions. We now explore the connection between tax base and revenue. Are smaller tax

bases in fact associated with reduced local government budgets? Or do low-tax base localities adapt


<!-- Page 326 -->


318

to their challenging circumstances by taxing their smaller base at higher rates, receiving transfers from

higher levels of government, or turning to other forms of revenue?

We address this question by merging our data on per capita tax base with Census of

Governments data on revenue by source in 2017 (the closest available time point to our appraised

value data). We run descriptive regressions of the association between (1) the percent of municipal

revenue and (2) the logged revenue per capita from each of several sources and the (logged) local tax

base per capita. Observations are individual jurisdictions, weighted by population. We include state

ﬁxed eﬀects to account for the unique institutional arrangements of each state and CBSA ﬁxed eﬀects

to account for the unique economic conditions in each metro area. To avoid double counting

properties contained within both a county and a municipal government, we focus on incorporated

municipalities (cities and towns) in the main text.

*Table 4.4 reports the total revenue raised by all municipalities in the U.S. from each source,*

then presents the coeﬀicients on logged tax base per capita as a predictor of the share (ﬁrst two

columns) and total amount (second two columns) of revenue from each source. A positive coeﬀicient

indicates that, relative to other municipalities in the same state and metropolitan area, municipalities

with higher tax bases receive more revenue from a given source; a negative coeﬀicient indicates the

opposite.


<!-- Page 327 -->


319

*Table 4.4. Results from regressions analyzing the relationship between logged per capita property tax base and amount of revenue raised by municipalities and towns from various sources.*


<!-- Page 328 -->


320

The ﬁrst line in Table 4.4 shows results of the regression predicting total revenue as a function

of property tax base. The coeﬀicient is 0.25 and highly statistically signiﬁcant. This indicates that, on

average, a 1 percent increase in tax base translates into roughly 0.25 percent more revenue per capita.

The coeﬀicient being less than 1 indicates that some substitution occurs: jurisdictions with higher

ﬁscal capacity choose to pay lower tax rates, and/or places with lower ﬁscal capacity derive greater

revenues from sources other than property taxation.

The second panel of Table 4.4 examines the relationships between the property tax base and

various forms of tax revenue. The coeﬀicients on the percentage of total revenue from all taxes and

from property taxes are positive and statistically signiﬁcant, meaning that they form a greater

percentage of municipal budgets in localities with larger property tax bases. In dollars, the coeﬀicient

on property tax revenue is 0.44, meaning that about half of a given diﬀerence in property tax base

between two municipalities (in the same state and metro) translates into a diﬀerence in property tax

revenue.

The third panel examines intergovernmental transfers. Overall, transfers form a larger

percentage of revenue in municipalities with smaller tax bases. These transfers are also mildly

redistributive: on average, a 1 percent decrease in a municipality’s tax base is associated with a 0.07

percent increase in transfers per capita. Federal transfers are strongly redistributive: a 1 percent

decrease in a jurisdiction’s tax base is associated with a 0.82 percent increase in the amount of federal

transfers received. This largely reﬂects federal transfers for housing and community development,

which are even more redistributive. But state transfers, which are a much more important component

of local revenue than federal transfers, are much less progressively distributed: a 1 percent decrease in

tax base is associated with just a 0.09 percent increase in state transfers. Transfers for education do

have a negative association with local tax base, meaning they are on average directed to poorer

jurisdictions. By contrast, state transfers for public welfare and transportation have positive


<!-- Page 329 -->


321

coeﬀicients (albeit not quite statistically signiﬁcant in the case of public welfare)—indicating that they

are directed in greater amounts to richer cities.

The fourth panel of Table 4.4 shows results for revenue from charges.  In cities with larger

tax bases, this category of revenue is higher in absolute terms, but comprises a similar proportion of

the budget. Charges from sewerage and solid waste management do not increase with tax base; they

form a larger percentage of the budget in poorer jurisdictions. Revenue from utilities, shown in the

ﬁfth panel, is higher, in absolute terms, in cities with smaller tax bases—water utility revenue stands

out as especially regressive, notable given increasing concerns about rising water costs (Mack & Wrase,

2017). Finally, the last panel shows revenue from other miscellaneous sources. All of these increase in

absolute terms with the size of a locality’s tax base, but ﬁnes and forfeitures form a larger percentage

of the budgets in poorer cities, consistent with previous research in metropolitan Chicago (Pacewicz

and Robinson 2021).

These regressions should be interpreted with some caution. The CBSA and state ﬁxed eﬀects

mean that the reported associations are driven by variation among municipalities in the same

institutional (state) and economic (metro) context. But these variables cannot entirely account for how

responsibilities are allocated to diﬀerent levels of government across diﬀerent states, or if some forms

of revenue are raised by only certain localities within a given metro. Moreover, states may diﬀer in the

quality of local government ﬁnancial data collected and reported to the Census of Governments.

Nonetheless, these regressions provide some initial evidence that municipalities with greater ﬁscal

capacity enjoy some of that beneﬁt through lower property tax rates and some through greater

revenue, while low-tax-base jurisdictions only partially compensate for their lower property tax

revenue through intergovernmental transfers, utility revenue, and ﬁnes.

## DISCUSSION

Metropolitan fragmentation is a characteristic feature of the United States political economy

(Freemark et al., 2020; Weir & King, 2021). The fragmentation of local governments has often been

theorized as a normatively positive feature, imposing ﬁscal discipline on local spending and allowing

residents to “vote with their feet” to select their preferred bundle of taxes and services (Tiebout, 1956).

But recent scholarship has questioned these theorized beneﬁts of fragmentation (Goodman, 2019;

Liscow, 2017), drawing greater attention to the ways in which local government fragmentation may

contribute—whether inadvertently or by design—to several of the most troubling social and economic

challenges facing the United States today.

We have contributed to this interdisciplinary literature by documenting one consequence of

the uniquely American combination of fragmentation and local revenue generation: the unequal

distribution of taxable property wealth across local jurisdictions. We have measured the taxable real

property wealth located within virtually every local government in the country—as understood by

those governments themselves, via their tax assessors—and calculated the extent to which

jurisdictional boundaries fragment metropolitan tax bases. As we have shown, tax base fragmentation

is a distinctive phenomenon, capturing important metropolitan variation that is missed by existing

measures of jurisdictional fragmentation and neighborhood-level segregation. Under the US ﬁscal

system, it operates as a ﬁscal constraint on local governments in parallel to legal constraints and voter

preferences.

Some of our ﬁndings align with widely held intuitions: the tax bases of metropolitan Detroit

and Bridgeport are highly unequal, Des Moines less so; the Hamptons are extraordinarily wealthy

while the city of Newark lacks ﬁscal resources. But the granularity and speciﬁcity of our data allow us

to undertake a systematic, nationwide analysis. We identify hundreds of small municipalities that

function as tax shelters—including dozens that have virtually no residents, but shield millions of


<!-- Page 331 -->


323

dollars in amassed corporate wealth from local taxation. At the same time, we document nearly one

thousand jurisdictions that are ﬁscally impoverished: jurisdictionally separated from the taxable wealth

that exists in their metropolitan areas, and facing ﬁscal challenges distinct in source if similar in

consequence from those facing localities in economically declining regions.

We believe this analysis opens major avenues for future work. Research in sociology and

economics has persuasively documented the importance of residential “place” for a range of social

and economic outcomes, including social mobility (Sampson, 2012; Sharkey & Faber, 2014). But in

the United States, the social and spatial dimensions of place are—uniquely—bundled with diﬀerent

packages of public goods that might also plausibly be associated with life outcomes. The data created

here at the metropolitan and municipal scales will allow researchers to begin disentangling the eﬀects

of ﬁscal resources, ﬁscal policy choices, and other aspects of spatial context.

The links between tax base fragmentation and racial inequality deserve particular attention.

White ﬂight has been a core driver of municipal fragmentation throughout U.S. history—including

current cityhood movements in Georgia, Louisiana, and elsewhere (Godinez Puig, 2024; Trounstine,

2018)—and the property tax has frequently been deployed to dispossess African Americans (Atuahene

& Berry, 2018; Henricks & Seamster, 2017; Kahrl, 2024). Our results highlight the role that the U.S.

system of decentralized funding responsibility may play in this process; future research should

continue to trace the connections between racism, segregation, ﬁscal federalism, and racial inequality.

The impacts of tax base fragmentation on local governments also merit further inquiry. Our

ﬁnding that municipalities with smaller tax bases rely more heavily on charges, utility revenue, and

ﬁnes and forfeitures is consistent with Pacewicz and Robinson’s (2021) research on the Chicago

suburbs; we hope that our data can facilitate similar analyses of other metropolitan areas, including

eﬀorts to establish causality. But there are broader consequences for jurisdictions that should also be


<!-- Page 332 -->


324

explored—for instance, tax base is included in municipal credit ratings (Norris, 2021), meaning that

tax base fragmentation directly shapes whether and at what cost municipalities can borrow.

Future research should also more fully probe the origins of tax base fragmentation, and how

it has changed over time.  The variation we have documented is shaped by known processes, including

municipal incorporation (Godinez Puig, 2024), selective annexation (Anderson, 2010; Zhang, 2024),

white ﬂight (Sugrue, 2014; Trounstine, 2018), and mobile corporate investment (Slattery & Zidar,

2020). Researchers should explore the relative contributions of these and other processes, and how

their importance varies around the country.

Tax base fragmentation, and its consequences, are structured by elective policy choices. In the

U.S., state law determines how easy or diﬀicult it is for localities to incorporate, secede, or resist

annexation by central cities. The reliance on locally generated revenue results from the decisions by

states and (especially) the federal government to limit ﬁscal transfers to localities. Government policy

also shapes the extent and patterns of economic segregation within metros. Alterations to these

policies could reduce the level of tax base fragmentation or ameliorate its consequences. U.S

policymakers might draw lessons from America’s brief experiment with general revenue sharing during

the 1970s (Wallin, 1998) and the two recent rounds of emergency federal aid to states, localities, and

tribal governments (Rocco & Kass, 2022). Another approach would be to centralize more spending

at higher levels of government, which is associated with reduced spatial inequality in mortality and

economic mobility (O’Brien et al., 2025, 2025).

Metropolitan areas in the United States contain enormous amounts of social and economic

inequality, which can seem impossibly durable. By highlighting how jurisdictional proliferation

interacts with economic segregation to fragment local ﬁscal capacity, we have shown that some

portion of this inequality derives from institutional design. A more equitable metropolis is entirely


<!-- Page 333 -->


325

feasible—but for as long as jurisdictional boundaries neatly segment the spatial distribution of taxable

wealth, achieving this result will require ﬁscal centralization.
